food.text: The baguette was brought to Vietnam by the French in the mid-19th century, during the Nguyễn dynasty, and had become a staple food by the early 20th century. In the 1950s a distinctly Vietnamese style of sandwich developed in Saigon and became a popular street food.

Singaporeans often eat at hawker centres, coffee shops or food courts rather than restaurants, for convenience, variety and affordability. Hawker centres usually feature dozens of stalls in one complex, each with its own speciality dishes. They have come to define Singaporean food culture.

The first domestically brewed beer in Cambodia was produced in the 1930s, during the French Indochina period, by the Brasseries & Glacières de L'Indochine company in Phnom Penh. In 2010 beer overtook spirits as the most popular alcoholic beverage in the country.

After the Fall of Saigon in 1975, bánh mì sandwiches became a luxury item once again. During the so-called subsidy period, state-owned phở eateries often served bread or cold rice as a side dish, leading to the present-day practice of dipping quẩy in phở.

Singapore's hawker culture was nominated in 2018 for UNESCO's Representative list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The nomination was submitted in March 2019 and inscribed on 16 December 2020. UNESCO described hawker centres as community dining rooms where people from diverse backgrounds share meals.

In December 2020, Cambodia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched a Food Diplomacy 2021–2023 campaign. Minister Prak Sokhonn listed dishes to promote, including prahok and fish amok. In February 2021 the ministry published a cookbook, The Taste of Angkor, for Cambodian diplomatic missions abroad.

Until the mid-20th century, most Chinese migrants to Cambodia were Teochews, with fewer Hainans, Hakkas and Cantonese. Today the Teochew kway teow is a popular Cambodian dish eaten for breakfast, lunch, dinner or as a snack, often flavoured with lime, chili, fish sauce and palm sugar.

In the 1980s, Đổi Mới market reforms led to a renaissance in bánh mì, mostly as street food. The word bánh mì was added to the Oxford English Dictionary on 24 March 2011, and Google celebrated it with a Google Doodle on 24 March 2020.

Cambodian annual beer consumption per capita was only around two liters in 1995, but it began to rise significantly by 2004. By 2019 a growing craft beer scene had 12 brewpubs or microbreweries operating in Cambodia.

On December 12, 2017, the Tuổi Trẻ newspaper and Acecook Vietnam Company organized the first Phở Day in Vietnam. Since 2018, Phở Day has been organized as a community cultural and tourism activity. In 2016 the Japanese had chosen April 4 as Vietnam's Phở Day in Japan.

Before 1975, well-known South Vietnamese bánh mì vendors included Bánh mì Ba Lẹ and Bánh mì Như Lan, which opened in 1968. After 1975, Ba Lẹ owner Võ Văn Lẹ fled to the United States and, with Lâm Quốc Thanh, founded Bánh mì Ba Lê.

A 1960 Cambodian cookbook, The Culinary Art of Cambodia by Princess Norodom Rasmi Sobbhana, was republished in May 2021 by Angkor Database. It was included in the government's food promotion campaign, and in May 2022 training facilities called Angkor Kitchen were unveiled.

art.text: Cambodia began a tradition of modern art in the mid-20th century. In the later 20th century both traditional and modern arts declined for several reasons, including the killing of artists by the Khmer Rouge. The country has since seen an artistic revival thanks to support from governments, NGOs, and foreign tourists.

Much of the 20th century art in Vietnam's National Museum of Fine Arts is concerned with folk narratives of a nation in defence. It draws on themes of martyrdom, patriotism, military strategy and overcoming enemy incursion. The museum also holds a small collection of late 20th and early 21st century painting by artists exploring abstraction.
art.source_title: Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts
tags: Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts

art.text: Modern Singaporean art is often tied to the rise of art associations, art schools, and exhibitions in the 20th century. The most famous artists were migrant Chinese painters of the Nanyang style in the 1950s. They drew on Western watercolor and oil painting as well as Chinese ink traditions, while depicting Southeast Asian subjects.

Vietnamese water puppetry arose in the 12th century, with puppeteers standing in water behind a split-bamboo screen. Because of strict restrictions on learning the art, it had nearly died out before the Maison des Cultures du Monde intervened in 1984. That help reinvigorated the genre.

Cải lương, a form of Vietnamese theatre, originated in the early 20th century and is more popular in modern Vietnam than tuồng and chèo. It has stayed adaptable to modern innovations and now includes electric guitar. It is accompanied by nhạc tài tử, a complex and partially improvised form of chamber music.

After the success of the August Revolution in 1945, Vietnamese theatre entered a new creative period. Plays were born in war zones to serve the resistance. During the resistance war against the US, theatre troupes took up the slogan "Tiếng hát át tiếng bom", and many productions praised heroes and female martyrs.

Balinese art is of Hindu-Javanese origin, growing from the work of artisans of the Majapahit Kingdom who expanded to Bali in the late 13th century. From the 16th until the 20th centuries, the village of Kamasan was the centre of classical Balinese art. Since the late twentieth century, Ubud and its neighboring villages have been regarded as the centre.

Singapore has a notable history of performance art. The state enacted a de facto ban on the art form for a decade, from 1994 to 2003. This followed a controversial performance artwork at the 5th Passage art space.

The Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts stands at 66 Nguyễn Thái Học Street in Hanoi, a site selected by painter Nguyễn Đỗ Cung in 1963. The building, built in 1937, was an abandoned Catholic girl's boarding house. Next door at No. 65 was an artists' colony.
art.source_title: Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts
tags: Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts

art.text: In the Philippines, the Manila Metropolitan Theater was built in 1931. The Progress of Medicine in the Philippines paintings were finished in 1953, and the International Rice Research Institute painting was completed in 1962. The Manila Mural followed in 1968.
tags: Progress of Medicine in the Philippines

art.text: The Philippines' Bonifacio Monument was created in 1993, and the Rizal Monument was completed earlier, in 1913. Among other landmarks, the University of Santo Tomas Main Building was rebuilt in 1927, with its Central Seminary Building built in 1933.

war.text: The fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942 was the largest surrender in British military history. Lieutenant General Arthur Percival surrendered Allied forces there to the Japanese, and about 130,000 Allied troops became prisoners of war.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

war.text: On 15 February 1942, Allied forces in Singapore under Lieutenant General Arthur Percival surrendered to the Japanese. About 130,000 Allied troops became prisoners of war, making it the largest surrender in British military history.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

war.text: On 7 and 8 December 1941, Japan launched near-simultaneous offensives against British and American territories in Southeast Asia and the Central Pacific. Action in the Southeast Asian theatre ended when Japan announced an intent to surrender on 15 August 1945.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

war.text: The Vietnam War (c. 1955 – 30 April 1975) was fought in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia between North Vietnam and South Vietnam and their allies, and it was a proxy war of the Cold War. Estimates of Vietnamese soldiers and civilians killed range from 970,000 to 3 million, and some 275,000–310,000 Cambodians, 20,000–62,000 Laotians and 58,220 US service members also died. The war was marked by brutal atrocities, including large-scale massacres such as Huế and Mỹ Lai, terrorism, indiscriminate bombings, rape, torture and persecution of ethnic minorities, and 20% of South Vietnam's jungle was sprayed with toxic herbicides that led to significant health problems. By 1975 all three countries had become communist.
Two major British warships, HMS Repulse and HMS Prince of Wales, were sunk by a Japanese air attack off Malaya on 10 December 1941. It was one of many Allied defeats in the first half of the war.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

war.text: From 19 to 20 January 1974, the Chinese and South Vietnamese navies fought near the Paracel Islands, near the end of the Vietnam War. The Chinese closed to tens of meters and aimed at command posts, and a South Vietnamese minesweeper's magazine exploded and its captain was killed by small-arms fire. 75 South Vietnamese soldiers and 18 Chinese sailors were killed. China won and took over the portion formerly held by South Vietnam, gaining full de facto control of the Paracels.

To counter U.S. airstrikes, Ho Chi Minh asked Mao in May 1965 for Chinese anti-aircraft units. Chinese troops in North Vietnam totaled over 320,000 between June 1965 and March 1968, peaking at 170,000 in 1967.

In the Battle of Malaya, Japanese forces met stiff resistance from III Corps of the Indian Army, the Australian 8th Division and British units. Japan's superiority in air power, tanks and infantry tactics drove them back, and the Allies were out of Malaya by the end of January 1942.
war.source_title: South-East Asian theatre of World War II

war.text: When the last Chinese troops withdrew from Vietnam in August 1973, 1,100 Chinese soldiers had been killed and 4,200 wounded during their years in North Vietnam. Chinese troop numbers had peaked in 1967 at 170,000, then dropped sharply in 1969-70, after Sino-Soviet relations took a decisive turn for the worse in 1968. Chinese aid to North Vietnam declined over 1969 and 1970, even though North Vietnam was, in the article's words, "still locked in a desperate struggle with the Americans."

The number of US military personnel in Vietnam jumped from 23,300 in 1965 to 465,600 by the end of 1967. Of 27 million draft-age men between 1964 and 1973, 40% were drafted, but only 10% were actually sent to Vietnam.

South Vietnamese forces reported that the warship Nhật Tảo was sunk in the Paracels battle, and 75 soldiers, including its captain Ngụy Văn Thà, were killed and 16 wounded. On 20 January 1974 the Dutch tanker Kopionella rescued 23 survivors of the sunken ship. Fifteen more soldiers who had fought on Quang Hòa island escaped in lifeboats and were found by fishermen on 29 January.

In 1976 Vietnam's government organized Gathering Teams to find the remains of its dead soldiers. From 1994 to 2012, 172,460 PAVN/VC bodies were found, including 15,989 in Cambodia and 14,549 in Laos. Even so, in 2022 nearly 200,000 PAVN/VC dead were still missing, their bodies never found, and another 300,000 bodies had been found but buried anonymously and never identified.

literature.text: Written Vietnamese today uses the Latin script-based Vietnamese alphabet. It represents native Vietnamese words, words of Chinese origin, and other foreign loanwords. Under French Indochina, chữ Quốc ngữ gradually became the current written medium of literature, ending the era of the two older scripts.

For almost all of Vietnam's history, Literary Chinese was the medium of all formal writing, until the early 20th century. It was used for official business, historical annals, fiction, verse and scholarship. It was then replaced by vernacular Vietnamese written in the Latin-based Vietnamese alphabet.

After declaring independence from France in 1945, the provisional government of the Empire of Vietnam adopted a policy of increasing literacy with chữ Quốc ngữ. The efforts were hugely successful, and the literacy rate jumped overnight.

Chữ Quốc ngữ was created in the seventeenth century but was not widely used outside missionary circles until the early 20th century, when the French colonial government mandated it in French Indochina. After Vietnam declared independence in 1945, its provisional government used it to increase literacy, and the literacy rate jumped overnight.

The French colonial authorities opposed Chinese writing for two reasons. It made administration more difficult for them, and nationalist literature was being circulated in the language. Both Literary Chinese and chữ Nôm were swiftly replaced by the Latin-based Vietnamese alphabet in the early 20th century.
Some Vietnamese leaders resisted the popularity of chữ Quốc ngữ as an imposition from the French. Others embraced it as a convenient tool to boost literacy.

Vietnamese intellectuals kept writing in Chinese until the early decades of the 20th century. The nationalists Phan Bội Châu and Phan Châu Trinh, and the principal of the Tonkin Free School, even used Chinese to write their attacks on education in Chinese and on the examination system.

The nationalist Phan Bội Châu (1867–1940) wrote in Literary Chinese and also used it to communicate while in Japan and China. He spoke neither Japanese nor Chinese, so written Chinese was his way of communicating.

Benedict Anderson, a former director of Cornell's Southeast Asia Program who concentrated on Indonesia, wrote the 1983 book Imagined Communities. It explored the origins of nationalism. His work on the Cornell Paper debunked the official story of Indonesia's 30 September Movement and the anti-communist purges of 1965–1966 that followed it, and led to his expulsion from Indonesia.

science.text: In 2007, an analysis of cut marks on two bovid bones found in Sangiran showed they were made 1.5 to 1.6 million years ago by clamshell tools. This may be the oldest evidence of early humans in today's Indonesia. It is also the oldest evidence of shell tool use in the world to date.

In 1997, anthropologist Jean Michaud proposed the term Southeast Asian Massif for the human societies living above roughly 300 metres in the southeast of the Asian landmass. It covers highlands overlapping parts of 10 countries. The indigenous population within these limits numbers approximately 100 million.

Public health figures for Laos show female life expectancy at birth of 70.7 years and male life expectancy of 67.4 years in 2025. Healthy life expectancy was 54 years in 2007. Government expenditure on health was about 4% of GDP in 2006.

A 2020 genetic study by Liu et al. focused on ethnic groups in Vietnam and found most sampled groups closely related to East Asians. Austronesian and Austroasiatic speaking populations in Vietnam and Southern China carried 89% to 96% East Asian-related ancestry, 94% on average.

A 2021 study of the ancestral composition of modern ethnic groups in the Philippines suggests that a distinctive Basal-East Eurasian ancestry originated in Mainland Southeast Asia around 50,000 BCE. Through multiple migration waves, it gave rise to both Oceanian (Papuan related) and East Asian lineages.

Early 20th century communist movement leaders of Vietnam were notably optimistic about technology under colonial rule. They predicted a blessed future in which automobiles and trains would no longer be uniquely Western.

politics.text: In March 1945, Japan overthrew the French administration in Indochina on 9 March and imprisoned its civil servants. Two days later the Nguyễn dynasty proclaimed independence for its protectorates, creating the Empire of Vietnam under Emperor Bảo Đại. It was nominally independent but actually a Japanese puppet state, and ended with Bảo Đại's abdication after Japan's surrender and the August Revolution led by the communist Việt Minh.

Japan's Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, a term first coined by Foreign Minister Hachirō Arita on June 29, 1940, was presented as a union for economic self-sufficiency and resistance to Western imperialism and Soviet communism. In reality, militarists and nationalists saw it as a propaganda tool to enforce Japanese hegemony. Japan ran the occupied economies strictly for raw materials, and a cabinet member declared, "There are no restrictions. They are enemy possessions. We can take them, do anything we want". The brutality of the Japanese military led many people in the occupied regions to regard Japan as worse than their former colonial rulers, and according to estimates about 100,000 Burmese and Malay Indian labourers died building the Burma-Siam Railway.

The Battle of Dien Bien Phu was the decisive victory of the Việt Minh over French forces, with fighting lasting until May 1954. By then Laos and Cambodia had already become independent in late 1953, and the State of Vietnam followed on 4 June 1954, though all remained members of the French Union.

In 1986, Vietnam's Sixth National Congress of the CPV introduced the Đổi Mới reform programme, encouraging private ownership and restructuring state enterprises to operate under market constraints. Five-year economic plans gave way to a socialist-oriented market mechanism. Vietnam achieved approximately 8% annual GDP growth between 1990 and 1997.

In 1963, the Mahayana Buddhist monk Thích Quảng Đức self-immolated, burning himself in the middle of a busy intersection in Saigon. It was an act of protest against the regime of South Vietnamese President Ngo Dinh Diem, a member of the Catholic minority who ruthlessly persecuted and suppressed the Buddhist community.

During the 1944–1945 famine in northern Vietnam, over one million people starved to death. It came during the Japanese occupation, which began when Japan invaded Vietnam on 22 September 1940 while the collaborationist Vichy French kept administering the colony. In that period the Viet Minh, a communist resistance movement, developed under Ho Chi Minh from 1941.

Vietnam joined the World Trade Organization on 11 January 2007 as its 150th member. This followed the end of the United States' economic embargo in early 1994 and years of fast growth after the Đổi Mới reforms.

A 1955 South Vietnamese nationality law automatically made Vietnamese residents of mixed Chinese and Vietnamese parentage South Vietnamese citizens. The number of ROC nationals in South Vietnam fell from 621,000 in 1955 to 3,000 by 1958. In 1963 the government relaxed its stance, and a new law let foreign-born Chinese choose between ROC nationality and South Vietnamese citizenship.

In 1950, Ho Chi Minh's government was recognised by the Communist governments of China and the Soviet Union, and Mao's government gave Ho's forces a fallback position and abundant weapons. In October 1950, the French army suffered its first major defeat at the Battle of Route Coloniale 4.

In his 2009 book The Art of Not Being Governed, James C. Scott of Yale University used the concept of Zomia to challenge a story about modernity. That story says people exposed to modern technology and the modern state will assimilate. Scott argued that upland tribes are instead conscious refugees from state rule, and that for two millennia they have been fleeing the oppressions of state-making projects in the valleys: slavery, conscription, taxes, corvée labor, epidemics, and warfare.
tags: The Art of Not Being Governed

politics.text: The Southeast Asian Massif and the related concept of Zomia describe highlands that have historically been beyond the control of lowland governments. Their ethnic minorities preserved local cultures by living far from state control. Historian Willem van Schendel coined Zomia in 2002. Historically, lowland empires also used these highlands as reserves of resources, including slaves, and as buffer spaces between their domains.

philosophy.text: In 1963, a Mahayana Buddhist monk named Thích Quảng Đức self-immolated in the middle of a busy intersection in Saigon, burning himself to death in public. It was an act of protest against the regime of South Vietnamese President Ngo Dinh Diem, a member of the Catholic minority who ruthlessly persecuted and suppressed the Buddhist community.

Islam is the most widely practised religion in Southeast Asia, with approximately 242 million adherents, about 42% of the population. The region has the highest number of Muslims of any global region, surpassing the Middle East and North Africa.

Singapore was found by the Pew Research Center to be the world's most religiously diverse nation. The Singapore-based Inter-Religious Organisation recognises 10 major religions, and Buddhism is the most followed, with 31.1% of residents identifying as adherents in the 2020 census.

Islam in Southeast Asia is marked by mysticism, and Sufism has a large regional following. Muslims there see adapting Islam to local traditions as a positive thing. In Indonesia, the dominant Abangan group practices a form of Islam that incorporates rituals inherited from their pre-Islamic ancestors.

After the communist takeover of Laos in 1975, some Buddhist monks feared the Pathet Lao government threatened Buddhism. Many fled to Thailand and helped fund resistance movements from across the border, while monks who stayed supported resistance fighters with food and medical supplies.

Cao Đài is categorised by the Vietnamese government as a form of Vietnamese indigenous religion. It brings together worship of the thần or local spirits with Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism, as well as elements of Catholicism, Spiritism and Theosophy.

Vietnamese folk religion was suppressed at different times in the 20th century. Debate and criticism of cultural destruction began in the 1960s, and by the early 1980s the state returned to preserving religious culture. The indigenous religion was soon promoted as the backbone of a progressive culture imbued with national identity.

K. M. Fozdar and Shirin Fozdar were the first to introduce the Bahá'í Faith to Singapore when they settled there in 1950. Shirin Fozdar was well known across Singapore and Asia for her work for women's emancipation. By 1952 there were enough Bahá'ís to form the first Local Spiritual Assembly.

Minh Lý Đạo was founded by Âu Kiệt Lâm (1896–1941), an intellectual of half Chinese and half Vietnamese blood, who was also a shaman. Its primary deities are the Jade Emperor and the Queen Mother of the West.

In the 1990s, a carpenter known as Master Thu in Hải Phòng's Vĩnh Bảo District claimed the spirit of the 16th-century sage Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm visited him at night. He built a shrine in 1996, and by 2016 the resulting movement, Minh Đường Trung Tân, had drawn more than 10,000 visitors and thousands of followers.

culture.text: Singapore is a secular state, yet analyses by the Pew Research Center found it to be the world's most religiously diverse nation. The Inter-Religious Organisation recognises 10 major religions there. Foreign workers from Indonesia, the Philippines and elsewhere add even more variety with their own congregations.

Islam is the most widely practised religion in Southeast Asia, with about 242 million adherents, roughly 42% of the region's population. Southeast Asia has more Muslims than the Middle East and North Africa. Islam there is often adapted to coexist with local traditions.

The most popular style of traditional Vietnamese clothing is the áo dài, a 20th century modernization of áo ngũ thân designed primarily for women. Vietnamese clothing was historically shaped by Chinese aesthetics, with Cham and later Western fashion, introduced through France, also leaving marks.

Vietnamese folk religion is not an organized system but a set of local worship traditions devoted to the thần, meaning spirits or gods. Ancestral veneration is practiced by most Vietnamese to varying degrees. About 86% of the population is reported as irreligious, yet many still follow these traditions.

Indonesia's government recognised only six religions in 1965, including Confucianism. A 1978 directive by the Minister of Home Affairs asserted there were only five, and in 1979 a presidential cabinet meeting decided Confucianism is not a religion. Schoolchildren were taught that there were only five official religions.

Under Indonesia's New Order regime, Confucianists were not recognised in practice by the government. They were forced to register with one of the five official religions to maintain their citizenship. This applied to the national registration card, marriage registration and family registration card.

In 2008, a festival in Huế performed the Nam Giao ceremony again, after it had been revived for the first time in 2004. Participants wore traditional clothing highlighting the Nguyễn dynasty, though the article says some of the Nguyễn dynasty costumes at the event were still inaccurate.
